Event_Names: Very Severe Cyclonic Storm (Bay of Bengal)
Time_Annotation: The storm originated from the monsoon trough on November 7 in the Bay of Bengal, east of India. Atypical for most November storms, the system continued to the north and dissipated over Nepal on November 11.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: In India, the cyclone's strong winds were accompanied by heavy rainfall and a storm surge that inundated the coastline. In neighboring Bangladesh, high waves killed 45 people after sinking or sweeping away four ships. The system later dissipated over Nepal and spawned a rare November snowstorm with avalanches and landslides.
Main_Event_Annotation: Reaching peak 3 minute winds of 120 km/h (75 mph), the IMD classified the system as a very severe cyclonic storm, indicating its tropical cyclone nature.
Hazards_Annotation: The cyclone produced strong winds and heavy rainfall, with associated storm surge leading to coastal flooding in India and high waves causing fatalities in Bangladesh.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In early December, following another outbreak of cold temperatures, a major winter storm impacted the far southern reaches of the United States – areas as far as the southern portions of the Gulf Coast up to the Mid-Atlantic states and New England received a wide swath of accumulating snowfall, significantly hampering travel and knocking power out to tens of thousands.[8]

Days later, a second nor'easter developed and rapidly strengthened while bringing heavy snowfall to New Jersey and interior New York. The storm caused up to 1 million people to lose power. Hundreds of flights were cancelled across the region, and many schools closed due to the nor'easter. Several municipalities in the Philadelphia area declared snow emergencies and many schools and government offices were closed on March 7.

The fourth and final nor'easter occurred on March 20 to 22, with its focus further south in the Mid-Atlantic. Some areas saw their heaviest late-season snowfall on record, and approximately 100,000 lost power as a result of the storm.[24]

Time_Annotation: A westward-moving tropical wave developed into Tropical Storm Erika late on August 24 while located about 1,035 mi (1,666 km) east of the Leeward Islands. After striking Florida on the following day, the remains of Erika became indistinguishable over Georgia on September 3.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Several Leeward Islands experienced heavy rainfall during the passage of Erika, especially Dominica. In Guadeloupe, heavy rainfall in the vicinity of Basse-Terre caused flooding and mudslides, forcing roads to temporarily close. Approximately 200,000 people in Puerto Rico were left without electricity. In the Dominican Republic, a weather station in Barahona measured 24.26 in (616 mm) of rain with significant damage to homes and displacement of people. Five people died in Haiti from weather‐related incidents. Shortly thereafter, the remnants trekked across Hispaniola and later Cuba.
Main_Event_Annotation: The article identifies the system as Tropical Storm Erika, indicating it falls under the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: The text details that several areas experienced heavy rainfall leading to catastrophic mudslides and flooding in Dominica and flooding with mudslides in Guadeloupe.

Event_Names: 2022 Eastern and Central Pacific Hurricane Season Forecast
Time_Annotation: On May 17, 2022, the Servicio Meteorológico Nacional (SMN) issued its forecast for the season, predicting a total of 14–19 named storms, 6–9 hurricanes, and 2–4 major hurricanes to develop. On May 24, 2022, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) issued their outlook, calling for a below-normal season with 10–17 named storms, 4–8 hurricanes, 0–3 major hurricanes, and an accumulated cyclone energy index of 45% to 100% of the median.

Time_Annotation: On August 30, the NHC noted that an area of disturbed weather had formed a few hundred miles south of Acapulco, Guerrero. Hazards_Annotation: Hazard evidence in the text includes sustained winds (85 mph over Socorro Island and gusts near 100 mph in parts of Southern California and southwest Arizona) and heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding (with rainbands drenching coastal states and flash flooding closing roads).

Total_Summary_Deaths.Total_Deaths_Annotation: Collectively, the tropical cyclones of the season resulted in at least 2,136 deaths. Individual events report 41 deaths in Jamaica (Tropical Depression One), 2 deaths in Texas (Tropical Storm Claudette), approximately 1,000 deaths in Dominican Republic (Hurricane David), an overall 2,068 deaths attributed to Hurricane David, 5 deaths in Greater Houston (Tropical Storm Elena), and 4 deaths (2 in Texas and 2 in Kentucky) from a mid/late‐September tropical depression.

Tropical Storm Elena brought flooding to the Greater Houston area, resulting in 5 deaths.
A tropical depression in mid and late-September caused flooding in the Southern United States, with 2 deaths reported in Texas.
The same mid and late-September tropical depression also resulted in 2 deaths reported in Kentucky.

Time_Annotation: After curving abruptly north-northwestward, Gloria became a hurricane early on September 7. During that time, Gloria slowly began merging with a low pressure area that was located north of the Azores and lost tropical characteristics by September 15.

Hazards_Annotation: Gloria moved west-northwestward at about 17 mph (27 km/h) and reached a peak with winds of 100 mph (155 km/h), indicating significant wind hazards.

Time_Annotation: Typhoon Higos developed on September 25 east of the Northern Marianas Islands. It tracked west‐northwestward for its first few days, steadily intensifying into a powerful typhoon by September 29. Higos weakened and turned to the north‐northeast toward Japan, making landfall in that country's Kanagawa Prefecture on October 1. Shortly thereafter, it crossed over Tokyo, becoming the third strongest typhoon to do so since World War II. It weakened while crossing Honshu, and shortly after striking Hokkaidō on October 2, Higos became extratropical. The remnants passed over Sakhalin and dissipated on October 4.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Due to cold sea surface temperatures and the typical track of most Pacific hurricanes, there has only been one recorded landfall of a tropical storm in the state – a storm in 1939 that hit Los Angeles, killing 45 people after catching many residents off guard.

Former Hurricane Kathleen in 1976 produced 14.76 inches (375 mm) of rainfall along Mount San Gorgonio and killed at least nine people in the state from heavy rainfall, with severe flooding affecting the city of Ocotillo.
Hurricane Guillermo in 1997, which killed a swimmer in Orange County.
Tropical Storm Nora in 1997 entered the state, producing gale-force winds and heavy rainfall that led to four traffic deaths.
The remnants of Hurricane Kay in 2022 produced flooding and 100 mph (160 km/h) wind gusts across southern California, killing one person.
In August 2023, the remnants of Hurricane Hilary produced 87 mph (140 km/h) winds along with heavy rainfall, with floods killing one person.

Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Inez struck the French overseas region of Guadeloupe on September 27; made landfall on the Barahona Peninsula of the Dominican Republic; struck southwestern Haiti; reintensified before striking southeastern Cuba on September 30; heavy rainfall and high tides caused flooding in the Bahamas; and at its final landfall, it flooded portions of Tamaulipas in Mexico.
Main_Event_Annotation: Inez developed from a tropical wave into Tropical Storm Inez on September 24 and strengthened into a hurricane — a progression typical of a Tropical Storm/Cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The storm attained peak sustained winds of 165 mph (indicative of severe wind hazards) and produced extensive flooding, as evidenced by the destruction of houses in the Dominican Republic and flood damage in the Bahamas and Mexico.

Main_Event_Annotation: The system was described as a depression that intensified and was named Storm Athina by Hellenic National Meteorological Service,[13][14] indicating it falls under the storm category. Based on the context and standard classification in the Mediterranean, it aligns with an Extratropical Storm/Cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: Record rainfall in Liguria (496 mm in Savona in just 6 hours) and the flooding of basements, turning roads into rivers, directly point to flood hazards.[15][16]

Time_Annotation: On September 20, METEOSAT imagery indicated an area of convection becoming concentrated while well south of the Azores. By the following day, satellite imagery noted a well-defined low-level circulation associated with Tropical Depression Five. The system was upgraded to Tropical Storm Charley on September 22, became a hurricane on September 23, peaked as a Category 2 hurricane on September 24, was downgraded to a tropical storm early on September 27, and finally merged with another extratropical low on September 29.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Later on September 27, Charley crossed over Terceira Island in the Azores, and the remnant system accelerated northeastward toward the British Isles.
Main_Event_Annotation: The storm evolved from Tropical Depression to Tropical Storm Charley on September 22 and then became a hurricane on September 23, classifying it as a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: While passing through the Azores, Charley produced tropical storm force winds, with Lajes AFB reporting sustained winds of 53 mph and gusts reaching 82 mph.

Locations: Between Del Dios Highway and State Route 56
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: On the morning of October 22, at 5:22 AM PDT, residents located between the Del Dios Highway and State Route 56 were ordered to evacuate.[34][10]
By 9:30 P.M. PDT on October 22, a dispatch from the city of Del Mar's web site stated: 'For your safety, we are strongly advising that all Del Mar residents evacuate.'[54]
Evacuations were also ordered for Scripps Ranch neighborhood, specifically 'Everything south of Scripps Poway Parkway, north of MCAS Miramar, east of Interstate 15, and west of Highway 67'.
The Mesa Grande Indian Reservation was evacuated due to the Witch Fire.[55]
Residents of the Barona Indian Reservation were advised to leave, though the evacuation was not mandatory; the casino on the reservation was closed.

At approximately 01:00 UTC on October 23 (6:00 PM PDT on October 22), fire broke out near Wildcat Canyon; residents of Wildcat Canyon and Muth Valley were ordered to evacuate, and the road was closed.[56]
At 9:50 P.M. PDT on October 23, 2007, the town of Julian, California was ordered to evacuate. Due to the fires, there was no power or phone service in the town.[57]

Time_Annotation: Early on June 16, sufficient development had taken place for the NHC to classify the wave as a tropical depression, at which time the depression was situated roughly 110 mi (175 km) south of Salina Cruz, Mexico. Hazards_Annotation: A scatterometer pass revealed peak winds of 35 mph (55 km/h), and significant flooding was evident when 82 homes in San Juan Bautista Tuxtepec were damaged by flood waters, with additional damage from high winds causing roofs to be lost and trees downed.

Hazards_Annotation: On September 21, Georgette attained its peak intensity with winds of 40 mph (65 km/h) indicating a wind hazard, and the event produced heaviest rains on Baja California Sur along with widespread flooding across affected regions.
